notes.title: Freedom and attention
notes.body: 自由自在 doubles the idea of freedom into a four-syllable phrase that sounds effortlessly complete. That opening freedom quickly turns into control over attention: everyone lies within his view, but nobody earns a reply. The enormous aerial perspective makes the petty insults that follow funnier; the narrator of the whole earth is still arguing with a particular “you.”

notes.title: A weaponized apology
notes.body: 不好意思 normally smooths a social awkwardness: excuse me, sorry about that. Here it introduces the announcement of coming first, so courtesy itself becomes a taunt. The winner acts as if other people’s embarrassment is an unfortunate inconvenience he politely acknowledges, while enjoying every moment of causing it.

notes.title: Recognition brings hostility with it
notes.body: 油然而生 is a polished four-character expression for a feeling springing up naturally. Dropping it between a sarcastic apology for winning and an obscenity makes the voice jump registers: formal explanation, schoolyard taunt, then bodily disgust. Success supposedly produces hatred as automatically as a chemical reaction.

notes.title: The taste of envy
notes.body: 酸 means sour, but it also describes envy in Chinese internet speech: someone else's success can leave a sour taste. The lyric pushes that taste into an exaggerated bodily image—sour enough to make your teeth fall out—immediately after boasting about coming first and attracting hate.

sources.label: People's Daily Overseas Edition: internet slang, 2019

phrase.en: so sour your teeth fall out

notes.title: Book, title, words
notes.body: A book is deep-fried, its title withers, and its words suffer from insecurity. The sequence judges a piece of writing by giving it the damaged body and emotions of its author. 油炸 also picks up the 油, yóu, in 油然而生 just before it: the character moves from a fixed expression into literal cooking oil, making the insult feel as if it is eating through the language.

notes.title: The writing tool turns violent
notes.body: The weapon is a pencil, following a ruined book, title and written words. Those everyday writing objects keep the violence inside the same imaginative world: language no longer just humiliates the opponent; its tools turn physically aggressive. The eye also answers the opening insults about blindness and the speaker’s own all-seeing view.

notes.title: Hehe. Not hehe.
notes.body: 嘻嘻 is the written sound of a giggle. The internet pairing 嘻嘻 / 不嘻嘻 flips instantly from amused to no longer amused, often after a nasty surprise. Placed after the pencil-and-blood threats, the cute giggle becomes cruel: the speaker supplies both the laugh and the moment it stops. The English needs a sentence to convey a switch Chinese makes by inserting one 不.

sources.label: Southern Weekly / Nanfang Plus: 嘻嘻不嘻嘻 (2024)

notes.title: Looking down, twice
notes.body: The song begins above the earth, looking down on everything; 瞧不起 then means regarding somebody as beneath you. English “look down on” preserves this movement from physical elevation to social contempt. The broad aerial view narrows into a refusal to recognize one particular “you.”

notes.title: A very talkative refusal

phrase.en: I ignore you, I ignore you

notes.body: 理 here means acknowledging, attending to, or engaging with someone. Each repeated refusal supplies a new reason, so “ignoring” becomes an entire sustained address. That contradiction is the hook’s pleasure: the speaker claims total indifference while spending the song making sure the rejected person hears it. English “ignore” keeps the action but softens this sense of withholding social recognition.

notes.title: A heart can move two ways
notes.original: 我才不管你心会动不动
notes.body: 心动, xīndòng, ordinarily means being emotionally stirred or attracted. This line pulls those words apart into a question about whether the heart can move at all. “Still beats” emphasizes bodily menace after the threats; the familiar emotional meaning remains audible underneath. The same heart can be treated as a vulnerable organ and the place where someone might still feel something.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 心動

notes.title: A double negative that demands respect

phrase.en: no choice but to give me my due

notes.body: 服 here means accepting someone’s ability or superiority, not merely obeying. 不服不行 literally says that refusing to acknowledge it will not do: the listener is denied even the option of withholding respect. It is a sharper boast than simply saying “I am good.”

notes.title: Warmth inside the clique
notes.body: 抱团取暖 pictures people pressing together against the cold. Its usual suggestion of solidarity turns sour beside “losers” and the next line’s resource-swapping: the circle provides protection and access, but only to its members. “Monoplay” repeats the phrase next to 小圈子, little cliques. Across both tracks, the complaint is about how belonging distributes support and opportunity.

notes.title: The business language of a clique
notes.body: 资源互换 sounds like the tidy language of networking or a mutually useful professional arrangement. Repeating “trash” before it strips that businesslike respectability away. The contrast matters: the lyric does not only accuse rivals of lacking talent; it pictures them maintaining a little exchange economy in which connections make up for what the music cannot do.

notes.title: A swear word can be praise
notes.body: 牛逼, niúbī, is vulgar praise: impressive, formidable, exceptionally good. Translating the body-part compound literally would miss its ordinary force. Its approving charge contrasts with the abusive 狗逼 earlier, showing how the same coarse ending can serve praise or contempt. Repetition turns it into a simple self-coronation after the elaborate reasons for withholding respect from everyone else.

notes.title: Showing your hand
notes.body: 摊牌 means laying one’s cards face up, hence revealing a position previously concealed. 我不装了 announces an end to pretending. After the long refusal to acknowledge anyone, this is a comic reveal with no hidden surprise: the supposedly secret truth is the boast he has already repeated. The performance of dropping a mask becomes another way to show off.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 攤牌

phrase.en: Cards on the table, I'm done pretending

tracks.intro: A victory speech delivered as a refusal to speak to anyone: sour envy, ruined writing, clique politics and a laugh that abruptly stops.

notes.title: The opening comes from “Nettles”
notes.original: Maybe you're right and we should stop watchin' the news (men—)
notes.body: The intro takes its two sung lines from Ethel Cain’s “Nettles.” In her Genius Verified explanation, Cain connects the song’s love to the fear of having someone to lose. Jackzebra’s refrain begins at that same emotional point, then changes the scale: the wish to protect one person becomes care for friends and family, preserved together in a picture scroll.

sources.label: Ethel Cain explains and recites Nettles — Genius Verified

notes.title: Brown eyes that look blue
notes.original: 'Cause, baby, I've never seen brown eyes look so blue
notes.body: “Blue” means sad as well as the color. The eyes remain brown; what changes is the grief visible in them. The color-word contradiction gives the sampled line its force, following the suggestion to stop watching upsetting news.

sources.label: Ethel Cain recites the line in Genius Verified, 07:30

notes.title: Gratitude built out of fear
notes.body: The refrain begins with fear, then answers it with a small practical verb: 珍惜, to cherish and take care of. It never promises that loss can be prevented. Repeating the four-line passage makes preservation into an ongoing practice—notice what is here, collect it carefully, then begin again. This is why the prayer feels protective rather than triumphantly secure.

notes.title: What is right in front of you
notes.body: 眼前 literally means “before the eyes,” joining what is physically near to what exists at the present moment. “What I have now” captures the time sense, but the Chinese also tells the speaker where to look. The song’s objects of care are close enough to see: scattered daily details, then the people around him.

notes.title: Every little drop
notes.original: 点点滴滴 / 小心翼翼
notes.body: 点点滴滴, diǎndiǎn-dīdī, gathers tiny, scattered details into an accumulation: little points and drops. The doubled syllables make that collecting audible. The next 小心翼翼 adds extreme care, so ordinary moments become fragile objects rather than background to a more important life. Repeating the refrain makes noticing them the song’s main activity.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 點點滴滴
Ministry of Education dictionary: 小心翼翼

notes.title: The fruits of effort
notes.original: 一切果实都来自我自己
notes.body: 果实 is both fruit and the result of effort, as in “the fruits of my labor.” The possessive claim briefly sounds like a conventional self-made boast. Its measure of achievement then changes: friends and family are doing well. The sequence lets earning and generosity coexist, rather than treating gratitude as a denial that the speaker worked for what he has.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 果實

notes.title: 幸福 is a kind of well-being
notes.body: 幸福 is happiness understood as a fulfilling life or fortunate condition, broader than the passing cheerfulness of 开心 in the previous line. Friends and family doing well make that condition visible. The English “blessed” brings out the gratitude and prepares the prayer, while the Chinese roots the feeling first in ordinary relationships.

notes.title: Effort becomes a gift
notes.body: 馈赠 is a more formal and generous word than an ordinary present; it stresses something bestowed. Coming only three lines after claiming the fruits of his own effort, it changes the emotional accounting. What he has earned can still feel given, because the happiness lies in a whole circle of people flourishing, something one person’s labor alone cannot guarantee.

notes.title: A shared future pictured as a scroll
notes.body: 画卷 evokes a painted scroll, giving the scene a form that can hold many people together. Writing everyone’s names onto it turns a pretty view into a record of relationships. The next promise is to preserve it and look after each person, so beauty becomes a responsibility. The image gives the earlier habit of collecting small moments a larger, shared container.

notes.title: A circle organized around care
notes.body: 照应 means attending to someone’s needs or helping when needed. It brings the grand picture scroll back to practical care: every name corresponds to a person who must not be overlooked. Across the mixtape, groups often appear as cliques trading advantages. This is a different model of a circle, organized around making sure nobody falls through.

notes.title: Names worth preserving
notes.body: 芳 literally evokes fragrance; 芳名 is an honorific way to speak of a name or good reputation. Alongside 永存, enduring forever, its elevated tone sounds almost like a dedication. The song moves from ordinary “friends and family” to words used to preserve someone’s memory, giving the prayer a shadow of loss even as it wishes them a good life.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 芳名

notes.title: Monsters can also be human threats
notes.body: 妖魔鬼怪 stacks four kinds of frightening supernatural beings into a familiar expression, also used for malign people or forces. The unexpectedly polite 请, “please,” asks them to keep their distance. That courtesy makes the protective wish tender and slightly childlike: immense dangers are addressed as though they might simply respect the boundary around his loved ones.

notes.title: The posture reverses the boast
notes.body: Here the speaker lowers himself to ask for protection for others. “Kai” later orders somebody else onto their knees; “Throat” returns to pleading before a Buddha. Kneeling changes meaning with who is speaking and who must kneel: devotion, dominance, and desperation are distinct uses across the mixtape.

notes.title: Prayer in the words and hands
notes.body: 您 is the respectful form of “you,” and it marks a new addressee after the song’s repeated “they.” The people being protected are no longer being described to us; protection is being requested from a higher power. 合十, joining the palms and ten fingers, has Buddhist associations, while 祈祷祷告 pairs two ordinary verbs for prayer. The scene gains reverence without naming a particular deity.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 合十
Ministry of Education dictionary: 祈禱

phrase.en: pray to you, pray to you

tracks.intro: A fear of losing everything becomes a patient inventory of what is worth keeping: ordinary moments, familiar names and the people behind them.

notes.title: The teacher becomes a salesman
notes.body: The pronouns stage a role: 老师我 is the teacher referring to himself, claiming the right to “handle” the pupil. At first the offense is merely 调皮, being naughty; within a few lines the same child is worthless, stupid and told to die. The escalation makes the adult’s language grotesquely disproportionate before the student’s destructive fantasy even begins.

notes.title: The discipline ruler
notes.body: 戒尺 is a ruler-like implement historically used by teachers to punish pupils. This one is described as iron. The following line specifies the palms and backs of the hands, making the classroom's authority physical and painful.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 戒尺

notes.title: Learning made physical
notes.body: 长记性 literally means to develop memory, but in a reprimand it means finally learning not to repeat a mistake. Coming immediately after the strikes to both sides of the hands, it turns “learning” into the memory of punishment rather than understanding a subject.

notes.title: Punishment at the threshold

phrase.en: stand by the door as punishment

notes.body: 罚站 compresses a punishment into one verb: being made to stand. The doorway places the pupil at the class’s boundary, visible but excluded from the lesson. Between blows to the hands and threats over exam results, this quieter detail shows another form of classroom power—controlling where the child’s body is allowed to be.

notes.title: The teacher’s grand vocation
notes.body: 教育事业 is elevated language for education as a profession or public undertaking. In the teacher’s mouth, “my” career matters more than the pupil’s welfare. The lofty noun is immediately followed by a very precise fee schedule. That collision of official-sounding purpose with private earnings is the verse’s central exposure.

notes.title: The threat becomes an hourly charge
notes.body: 补课 means supplementary or make-up lessons. This teacher makes the child’s survival conditional on attending paid classes at his own home. The conflict has a concrete institutional background: a 2015 Education Ministry notice explicitly prohibited serving schoolteachers from inducing pupils into paid tutoring. The satire exposes how authority over a child’s grades can become leverage over the family’s money.

sources.label: Education Ministry: prohibition on paid tutoring by serving schoolteachers (2015)

notes.title: The price of surviving class
notes.original: 一小时两百一个月一结

phrase.zh: 一小时两百一个月一结
phrase.en: Two hundred an hour, paid monthly

notes.body: After extravagant threats, the voice suddenly becomes an invoice: hourly rate, then settlement period. The plain administrative precision is part of the cruelty. It makes the impossible bargain sound routine and manageable, as though paying on time could resolve a system that has already declared the child disposable.

notes.title: Borrowing the family’s authority
notes.body: The teacher recruits parental disappointment after specifying his fee. A familiar appeal to family pride now works as the final push in a sales pitch. The line makes shame portable: even outside the classroom, the pupil is asked to carry the teacher’s demand home and experience it as an obligation to the parents.

notes.title: A schoolyard song with a dark second life
notes.body: The hook remakes 上学歌, a cheerful Going to School Song, through a playground parody circulated by children long before this recording. A 2007 school report describes the explosive-schoolbag version while condemning such songs and organizing replacement singalongs. That history sharpens the joke: even the supposedly childish escape fantasy became something adults tried to discipline.

sources.label: Tongling Daily: a primary school’s campaign against playground parodies (2007)

notes.title: A greeting that stays cheerful
notes.body: The little bird’s repeated morning greeting is deliberately simple, friendly and easy to sing. It stands opposite the adult’s dense sequence of insults and transactions. Retaining that bright nursery-song diction while changing the schoolbag preserves the pleasure of a children’s chorus, which makes its revenge fantasy more unsettling than a uniformly grim verse.

notes.title: A schoolbag becomes an explosive
notes.body: The decisive substitution comes at 炸药包: a bag of explosives takes the schoolbag’s place. The sun, flowers and bird have continued their cheerful routine, so the destruction enters through the object that normally signals obedient attendance. Keeping the nursery-song setup intact makes the rupture work; the world still smiles while the child imagines removing school from it.

sources.label: Zhengzhou Evening News / China News: the school-song rewrite

notes.title: The pupil’s rebellion starts giving orders

phrase.en: You've got to hear what I say

notes.body: The repeated 有什么不能 asks what could possibly be forbidden; 你要 then turns that freedom into commands directed at an audience. The voice changes from being handled to insisting on being heard and seen. Its rebellion adopts the same commanding grammar as the teacher, suggesting how thoroughly the classroom has supplied the available language of power.

notes.title: An anatomical “eye”
notes.body: 马眼 literally says “horse eye,” but it is slang for the opening at the tip of the penis. “Pisshole” carries both the anatomy and the coarse register. Two lines earlier, 狗眼 is an insult directed at someone’s eyes; 马眼 repeats 眼 while moving to a different body part. The sequence then shifts into pixelation and an impossible autopsy.

sources.label: Urologist Li Hongjun: the anatomical meaning of 马眼

notes.title: A censored image after the threat
notes.body: 马赛克 literally means mosaic; in media language it also means pixelation used to obscure part of an image. The line turns the preceding violent image into something one cannot clearly see, before the next line says even an autopsy is impossible. It changes from bodily detail to the image that might be left on a screen.

notes.title: Extreme violence, casual grammar
notes.body: 做不了一点 uses 一点, “even a little,” for emphatic total impossibility. After the image dissolves into mosaic pixels, the punchline is that no examination can recover it. The casual, almost conversational degree-word shrinks an extreme bodily image into an offhand judgment—the same deadpan mismatch that drives the teacher’s opening speech.

tracks.intro: A teacher’s sales pitch gives way to a schoolyard parody. The cheerful sun shines over threats, tuition fees and a child’s fantasy of making the whole institution disappear.

notes.title: Calling it all discipline
notes.body: 统称 is the act of grouping different things under one name. Repetition makes 纪律 sound like a label stamped onto whatever happens next. The verse then supplies its contents: beatings, scolding, stiff movements and false smiles. The accusation sits in the gap between the tidy name and the experience it is asked to make acceptable.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 統稱

notes.title: Care is withheld
notes.body: 谈心 suggests private, sincere conversation about someone’s concerns. The opening withholds precisely that kind of attention, then accuses the ignored person of seeking notice. Before rules become physical punishment, the song shows an emotional hierarchy: the person can be managed or dismissed, but does not get to explain what is happening inside.

notes.title: A little attention becomes an offense
notes.body: 点 makes the request small: a bit of attention. Set after three statements that nobody cares or even mentions this person, the charge of attention-seeking turns neglect into the neglected person’s fault. That circular logic gives the verse’s “discipline” an intimate cruelty before it expands into crowds and systems.

notes.title: Miracles leave; discipline stays
notes.body: Miracles are scarce, and then the magician goes home: the wording moves from something supernatural to somebody who performs illusions. What remains receives the name “discipline.” Read together, the lines let that tidy label replace any promise of transformation or rescue.

notes.title: People as loose sand
notes.body: Loose sand is an established idiom for people who cannot hold together as a group. Each grain remains separate. Placing it after 体系, 'system,' sets up the verse's tension: organization promises cohesion, while the next lines show the punishment used to enforce it.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 一片散沙

notes.title: The next punishment is waiting

phrase.en: After the beating comes the scolding

notes.body: 挨 marks being on the receiving end: first blows, then verbal abuse. The repeated structure makes punishment a sequence with another stage waiting after the first is over. It also undoes any comforting distinction between correcting behavior and humiliating a person; the system delivers both in the same grammatical rhythm.

notes.title: A crowd under one palm
notes.body: A dense crowd is reduced to something that fits beneath a palm. The scale makes domination almost tactile, and the stiff movements that follow make the people resemble controlled figures. No controller needs to be named for the arrangement to be clear: many bodies move inside the reach of one hand.

notes.title: The face obeys too
notes.body: After the stiff movements, even an expression of happiness looks rehearsed. Discipline has reached the face: the group does not only have to move correctly, but to appear content while doing it. The later reassurance “don’t be afraid” inherits this suspicion, since the words of comfort may be another required performance.

notes.title: Keep going / fill the tank
notes.body: 加油 means adding fuel and is also the everyday cheer 'keep going!' or 'come on!' Here the question separates 油, 'fuel,' from 加, 'add.' The coming car scene makes refueling literal, while the encouragement meaning creates an uneasy echo beside the trembling legs.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 加油

notes.title: The body contradicts the speech
notes.body: The mouth keeps talking while the legs keep shaking. Those simultaneous bodily actions separate the confident public statement from the fear that cannot be controlled. The doubled 一直, “all the time,” gives both equal duration: the speech does not stop the tremor, and the tremor does not interrupt the speech.

notes.title: Passengers without control
notes.body: This is an arrangement of power in miniature. Someone unable to see still occupies the driver’s seat; the “we” has a seat but no steering wheel. Following the crowded group under one hand, the car brings collective danger into an ordinary enclosed space where the passengers must entrust movement to somebody else.

notes.title: The spontaneous-trip slogan
notes.body: 说走就走的旅行 became a familiar phrase for the freedom to drop everything and travel; a 2015 China Tourism Academy speech discussed it as a youth buzzword. Here the passengers sit behind a driver who cannot see. The cheerful slogan lands inside a scene where they have little control over where they are going.

sources.label: China Tourism Academy: Dai Bin on the phrase at COTTM2015

phrase.en: A trip where you just get up and go

notes.title: Reassurance turns into an order

phrase.en: Whatever you do, don't look back

notes.body: 千万 intensifies the instruction into an urgent warning. Repeating “don’t be afraid” has not made the ride safe; the final command instead limits what the passengers may look at. The travel slogan returns after this warning, now sounding less like freedom than being carried along despite fear.

tracks.intro: A neat official word covers a frightening sequence: punishment, rehearsed smiles, trembling passengers and a driver who cannot see.

notes.title: A vulgar word used as a boast
notes.body: 屌 is profane but, used as an adjective, praises someone as impressive or formidable. 屌不屌 is the affirmative-negative question pattern: impressive or not? The speaker asks for a verdict and immediately asks again. That dependence on applause sets up a song about what happens when a performer’s sense of worth is put entirely in an audience’s hands.

notes.title: The performer becomes a commodity
notes.body: The insult makes a performer into someone selling bodily availability to music. The next lines give money and fame the power to enter without protection. This is deliberately sexualized humiliation, and its mechanism is specific: the performer who seems to command a stage becomes the exposed object of other people’s demands.

notes.title: Applause turns into a burial image
notes.body: Flowers and applause initially look like rewards for a performance, but they already cover a body. Later the same body acquires a tombstone, coffin and burial clothes. The sequence turns celebration into preparation for disposal, with almost no change of props. Fame does not protect this performer; it supplies the decorations for the ending.

notes.title: Success enters without protection
notes.body: Money and fame are personified as partners who do not have to use protection. That grotesque privilege explains the later language of parasites and disease: success enters the body without limits. The verse builds a sustained metaphor of exposure, rather than switching randomly from celebrity to medical imagery.

notes.title: The ego has its own appetite
notes.body: 寄生 is to live parasitically inside or upon a host. Conceit is given its own appetite, fed by the surrounding praise while the person beneath it loses desire. The irony is that the supposedly powerful ego is not the performer’s strength: it is another thing living off the performer.

notes.title: Flattery as a life companion
notes.body: 泡 is to soak or steep. Praise becomes a liquid environment the person will inhabit for the rest of a life, rather than a momentary burst of applause. Paired with 共度余生, language suited to lifelong companionship, it makes hollow flattery a suffocating substitute for an actual relationship.

notes.title: A fresh insult at the grave
notes.body: The tomb has an offering, but the expected flowers or drink are replaced with a bucket of urine. 热乎, still warm, is an everyday word that can make food sound fresh and comforting; here it makes the insult disgustingly immediate. The detail continues the song’s reversal of honors into humiliations, down to what is placed before the grave.

notes.title: A snack rhyme becomes a funeral sales pitch
notes.body: 切克闹 is a playful Chinese sound-spelling of “check it out.” Paired with 来一套, it remakes the familiar jianbing snack chant: the vendor’s complete set is now a coffin with burial clothes. The bouncy street-food sales rhythm makes the funeral goods sound like an irresistible everyday deal. A Nankai Youth League food article documents the original rhyme in circulation in 2017.

phrase.en: Yo, yo, yo, check it out

notes.title: The same character in two different transactions
notes.body: 套, tào, changes jobs across the song. 戴套 means wearing a condom; 一套 is a matching set; 圈套 later means a trap. The recurring sound links sex, funeral merchandise and deception. English needs three unrelated words, so the translation cannot reproduce the way a single syllable keeps wrapping itself around the performer’s fate.

notes.title: Being told what to want

phrase.en: Everyone wants you to want it

notes.body: The repeated 要 is the point: everybody wants, and what they want is for you to want. A personal desire is manufactured by collective pressure. Coming between a funeral sales pitch and commands about how to moan, cry and grin, the line makes the performer’s last private refuge—what they actually feel—part of the show.

notes.title: A ritual turned into a performance insult
notes.body: 跳大神 names spirit-invoking ritual performance involving dancing and incantation, traditionally associated with seeking protection or driving away misfortune. The lyric adds an obscene performance instruction to it; “Kai” later uses the same expression inside its grotesque caveman image. That sacred-to-derisive shift matters more here than the literal act of dancing.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 跳大神

notes.title: Pain must remain entertaining

phrase.en: When you cry, you have to grin

notes.body: 必须 is an uncompromising “must.” Grief is allowed only if the face still entertains, so the command produces a grotesque mask with pain behind it. The next two lines explain the business model: cornering the person creates the conditions for someone else to earn. That link makes the forced grin an image of exploitation, not simply emotional contradiction.

notes.title: The sales pitch keeps rhyming
notes.body: The second half rides a chain of open -ao sounds: 闹, nào; 套, tào; 笑, xiào; 钞票, chāopiào; 高考, gāokǎo. They bind the imported “check it out,” funeral package, forced grin, earnings and exam scene into one chant. English preserves the connections in meaning, but Chinese lets the grotesque sales pitch keep selling itself through rhyme.

notes.title: Banknotes compared with school papers
notes.body: The gaokao is China’s national college entrance exam. Photographs document students celebrating its end by throwing study materials into the air. The preceding stacks of cash borrow that image of paper suddenly released from its ordinary value. Schoolwork becomes confetti in one scene, money in the other; both produce a spectacular shower above the people below.

sources.label: China Daily — students tossing study materials after the gaokao (2013)

notes.title: One more meaning of 套
notes.body: 圈套 makes the plot’s shape explicit: a setup that catches someone. Earlier questions offered choice—do you want it?—but the crowd then insists that the answer must be yes. By the time the word “trap” arrives, desire, acclaim and even the funeral package have become things imposed on the person who is supposedly choosing.

notes.title: Disgust has a literal smell
notes.body: 狗屁, gǒupì, literally says “dog fart,” but its ordinary insulting force is “nonsense” or “bullshit.” English exchanges one bodily image for another. After all the persuasive forms the song has tried—acclaim, promises, offers, instructions—the repeated dismissal strips them of authority. The grand social performance ends as worthless noise.

notes.title: A written stand-in for a swear
notes.body: 草 is pronounced cǎo, close enough to the swear 操, cào, to stand in for it in informal writing. On the page it says “grass”; in this sequence it functions as a stream of cursing. After the patterned sales rhymes and elaborate insults, the language finally strips down to an almost percussive refusal.

tracks.intro: Applause becomes a funeral arrangement, a snack chant sells burial clothes, and every promise of pleasure turns out to have someone else’s price attached.

notes.title: A face you deliberately put on
notes.body: 挂脸 or 挂着脸 describes visibly wearing a displeased, stern, or unfriendly expression. It is an outward social signal, rather than necessarily an emotionless “poker face.” The proverb about dignity later lets 脸 move from a visible expression to the standing a person protects.

notes.title: Holding up a piece of sky

phrase.en: hold up my own piece of sky

notes.body: 撑起一片天 pictures supporting a whole space above oneself. As a figurative phrase, it suggests taking responsibility or establishing a place where one can stand independently. Beside earning little but refusing deception, the boast concerns sustaining a life on one’s own terms.

notes.title: Knowledge has an ethical limit
notes.body: The expected payoff of acquiring knowledge would be competence or income. Here it is followed by a refusal to deceive, even if that means earning little. The verse establishes an ethical limit before it begins flaunting artistic lawlessness: refusing a scam and refusing restraint are presented as compatible forms of self-respect.

notes.title: Face means dignity
notes.body: This is a variant of the proverb that people have faces as trees have bark: a person needs dignity and a sense of shame. Following the refusal to deceive for money, it makes 'face' a matter of self-respect. The title can therefore resonate with both facial expression and social standing.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 人有臉樹有皮

phrase.en: Trees need bark; people need their dignity

notes.title: Directing the scene
notes.body: The wish to direct a film is immediately realized in words: people enter a pot, the rules belong to the speaker, and so does the script. The grotesque scene reads as a declaration of artistic control. “This is art” then works as its punchline—the director claims the authority to call even his ugliest invention art.

notes.title: Familiar—and cooked
notes.original: 这样不用社交软件就能自来熟
notes.body: 自来熟 describes someone who becomes familiar with strangers immediately. The pivot is 熟, shú, which means both 'familiar' and 'cooked.' Put people in a boiling pot and they will get 'familiar' without a social app: the line makes a social idiom literal as a gruesome joke.

notes.title: No limit—and then a temperature
notes.body: 度, dù, can mean a degree, a measure, or a proper limit. Here jokes have no 度; a few lines later 温度, wēndù, explicitly names temperature, inside a sequence about boiling and heat. The same character links social restraint to the physically excessive cooking joke.

notes.title: The author owns the rules
notes.body: In “Discipline,” rules organize frightened people beneath somebody else’s hand. Here the first person claims authorship of rules and content together. The repetition of 我, “I,” makes control audible, but its setting inside an absurd cooking scene keeps the boast theatrical: this is the miniature world the rapper can make in a verse.

notes.title: Nothing left to fear
notes.body: 死猪不怕开水烫 says that a dead pig no longer fears being scalded. It describes someone beyond intimidation, often because they have lost any shame. Following the earlier insistence that people need dignity, the proverb introduces its unruly opposite. The face must be protected, yet artistic bravado also claims the freedom of someone with nothing left to lose.

sources.label: Hanzi dictionary: 死猪不怕開水燙

phrase.en: A dead pig that isn't scared of boiling water

notes.title: Hiding a face, displaying a pose
notes.body: The face that began the song becomes hard to see. 帽子, head lowered, and uninterrupted walking give aloofness a physical routine. The next repeated joke about looking cool exposes that routine as a recognizable pose, so the image both protects the speaker from others and offers them something to admire.

notes.title: Swagger described from outside
notes.body: 装逼 means putting on airs or performing impressiveness, with a coarse, mocking edge. “So cool” praises the very thing 装逼 discredits, leaving the pose both ridiculous and attractive. The preceding hat-down walk is a ready-made image of aloofness. The refrain lets us enjoy that image while noticing how hard it works to look effortless.

notes.title: Designer names take the place of objects
notes.body: “Commes” and “ricks” are fashion shorthand for Comme des Garçons and Rick Owens. They enter the verse without explanation, like items an initiated listener is expected to recognize. The repeated “I got” makes labels, people, love and pain grammatically equivalent possessions; the inventory grows beyond clothes without changing its structure.

notes.title: YoungQueenz is OZMA
notes.body: OZMA is a name YoungQueenz uses on his own Bandcamp and SoundCloud profiles. The paired “young zeebra / young ozma” places the two collaborators inside the same rolling list. It also shifts from ordinary possessions to identities: the verse can announce who they are with the same economy it uses to name what they have.

notes.title: What the inventory cannot filter
notes.body: Pain receives exactly the same “I got” construction as clothes, girls and love. That repetition prevents the boast from becoming a clean account of prosperity. The verse can accumulate everything wanted and still accumulate hurt; its quick refusal of enemies is the first item it decisively excludes from the collection.

notes.title: The easier choice is reversed

phrase.en: Keeping going is easier than giving up

notes.body: The expected motivational comparison makes perseverance harder and quitting easier. YoungQueenz reverses it: continuing is now the easier action. Beside the catalog of things he has and places he tours, the reversal sounds like momentum or commitment becoming habitual.

tracks.intro: Face means expression, dignity and pose. Jackzebra cooks social language into gruesome jokes, then YoungQueenz answers with an inventory of possessions, feeling and momentum.

notes.title: A deadline made into a refrain
notes.body: 年底 makes time itself a source of pressure: the year is closing and a balance needs to be settled. The recurring demand is unusually concrete for a money song. The speaker is neither shopping nor counting surplus wealth; he needs to recover money already earned. When the opening returns after the revenge fantasy, the account is still unresolved.

notes.title: Standing out while hiding
notes.body: The long hair first conceals his eyes, a defensive advantage, yet he immediately says he is too conspicuous to walk freely outside. The boast of standing out and the wish to escape hostile attention coexist in the same appearance. That tension complicates the apparent swagger: visibility offers status but also makes the body feel exposed.

notes.title: Envy accumulates into hate
notes.body: The phrase stacks three related reactions: admiration or envy, jealousy, then hatred. English “envious haters” compresses the escalation. 小人 adds a moral judgment: petty or dishonorable people, rather than physically small people.

notes.title: Contempt as public mess
notes.body: 随地大小便 is the blunt phrase used for urinating or defecating indiscriminately in public. Transferring it to jealous people makes their reaction sound like contamination of a shared space. It turns social hostility into a disgusting failure of basic restraint, extending the verse’s dog imagery before the yapping mouth appears.

notes.title: A swaggering plural
notes.body: 老子 literally says “father,” but here it is an aggressive first-person self-reference, as if the speaker outranks the person addressed. Adding 们 makes that swagger plural. English profanity preserves the roughness but loses the implied hierarchy: this “we” announces that nobody else gets to speak down to them.

notes.title: A mouth turned into a dog’s mouth
notes.body: 狗嘴 turns the opponent’s mouth into a dog’s; 叭叭 imitates its relentless noise. Together they deny the chatter the dignity of an argument. Across “Sour” and “Voices,” mouths and speech also become bodily irritants. Here “yapping” preserves both the canine insult and the sense of someone producing sound without offering repayment.

notes.title: The debt vocabulary turns violent
notes.body: 欠 means owing or lacking; 欠打 is the insulting judgment that someone deserves a beating. The same character used for money owed in the hook now makes a beating sound like another outstanding balance. “Begging for” gives the English idiom, but loses that shared debt vocabulary.

notes.title: Money that was hard to earn

phrase.en: Making money isn't easy for me either

notes.body: This is a sudden appeal to fairness inside a stream of insults. 也, “either,” assumes the listener knows earning is difficult too; 你也不是不知道 adds that they cannot plead ignorance. The debt is thus more than a missing sum. It shows someone refusing to recognize the labor of a person whose circumstances they already understand.

notes.title: The second job of getting paid

phrase.en: Collecting debts, collecting debts, collecting debts

notes.body: 讨 means demanding or seeking what should be given. Repeating 讨债 makes recovery sound like another job, one that has to be done every day after the original work of earning the money. The hook’s insistence is exhausting by design: nothing advances because the same request still has to be made.

notes.title: Debt also means favors owed
notes.body: 人情债 is a debt created by a favor, help or the obligations of a relationship. Unlike cash, it has no agreed unit or clear repayment date. Introducing it after the relentless literal debt-collection hook expands the grievance: the speaker is keeping track of unreturned loyalty as well as unreturned money. Every relationship threatens to become another account to chase.

notes.title: Courtesy is revoked
notes.body: 随你 would grant the other person their choice. The negation revokes that small courtesy, following a song full of requests the debtor has ignored. The verse now mirrors the lack of control it resents: unable to obtain voluntary repayment, the speaker fantasizes about taking every decision away from the other person.

notes.title: Revenge gets an appointment

phrase.en: a good day, a good time

notes.body: Choosing a good day and time sounds like arranging a welcome event. Its placement before the vehicular threat makes the politeness of scheduling grotesque. The revenge is given the practical calm denied to the rest of the speaker’s life, as though even an extreme fantasy can be entered neatly into a calendar.

notes.title: A poisoned success slogan
notes.body: 梦想实现 is the affirmative language of aspiration fulfilled. Here it names the completion of a revenge fantasy, shrinking the horizon of a better life to the removal of one enemy. The return to “pay me back” prevents that fantasy from resolving the song: imagined victory still leaves the ordinary demand unanswered.

tracks.intro: A demand for repayment expands into an angry ledger of work, favors, recognition and revenge. The hook keeps dragging every fantasy back to the unpaid money.

notes.title: Pressure as big as a mountain
notes.body: 压力山大 means pressure as huge as a mountain, but it also sounds like 亚历山大, the Chinese form of Alexander. A 2011 vocabulary study records that sound-play. The phrase makes stress into a ready-made joke; repeating it beside “who can I tell?” lets the joke carry real isolation.

sources.label: Aichi University, Japanese–Chinese Vocabulary Studies 1 (2011), pp. 63–71

notes.title: Looking for the right listener
notes.body: 心里话 literally means the words inside one’s heart, the things said sincerely rather than for display. Repeating the question of whom to tell makes the track search for an addressee. It is a revealing counterpoint to the many songs ordering others to be quiet: speech becomes valuable when it might finally carry something private.

notes.title: Begging everyone in sight
notes.body: 求爷爷告奶奶 literally distributes the pleading between grandpa and grandma. As an idiom it means asking anyone who might help, with a strong sense of lowering oneself and exhausting possible connections. The next line cancels the whole effort: not one of those people can be trusted. The complaint is as much about humiliating dependence as loneliness.

notes.title: Playing music to a cow
notes.body: 对牛弹琴 means playing a string instrument to a cow: effort wasted on an audience that does not understand. The older fable also concerns the mismatch between expression and listener. In a song about asking who can hear one’s private thoughts, the musical image is especially pointed. The speaker is not merely talking to a wall; the very thing he makes fails to communicate.

sources.label: Ministry of Education idiom dictionary: 對牛彈琴

notes.title: Space is supposed to make things beautiful
notes.body: This familiar formulation says distance produces beauty: too much proximity can spoil an idealized view. Here it follows “leave me alone” and precedes “nobody understands me.” The speaker asks for separation while also wanting to be understood, giving the polished saying an uneasy place in the verse.

notes.title: The insult turns inward
notes.body: 瞎 and 乱 both make the noise directionless; 几把 adds a coarse intensifier, and 叫 can be a human shout or an animal cry. The translation chooses “bark” because the next image makes the speaker a dog. The lyric briefly calls its own performance nonsense, then turns that unruly sound into determination.

notes.title: A dog without an owner
notes.body: 野狗 belongs to no household and has no owner to obey. Earlier songs use dogs to degrade enemies; here the speaker claims the animal for himself. After begging has failed, dependence is exchanged for feral persistence. The next line gives that persistence its object: the beat becomes something to chase and seize, even when human listeners offer no understanding.

notes.title: Holding on to the beat
notes.body: 死着咬 intensifies the grip: bite with everything and refuse to release. 伴奏 is the instrumental backing, so this animal violence is redirected into the physical work of rapping. The ending answers the opening problem of having nobody to confide in. The beat may not reply, but it is something the voice can keep engaging.

phrase.en: Chasing down the beat, biting and never letting go

tracks.intro: Stress becomes a meme, failed communication becomes an animal fable, and a stray dog finds the one thing it can hold onto: the beat.

notes.title: Too tired even to overthink
notes.original: 没有心思再去胡思乱想

phrase.zh: 没有心思再去胡思乱想
phrase.en: I don't have the headspace for wild thoughts anymore

notes.body: 心思 and 胡思乱想 repeat 思, thinking, but give it different forms: attention available for a task versus thoughts running out of control. The line says there is no energy left even for overthinking. That tired precision opens a song full of instructions about what to hear, say, ignore and keep secret.

notes.title: Scheming against one another
notes.original: 早过了勾心斗角的年纪
notes.body: 勾心斗角 means competitive maneuvering and intrigue. The speaker declares himself beyond its “age,” treating scheming as an immature phase one should outgrow. Yet the advice that follows assumes a world full of hostile speech. The opening is less a claim that conflict has disappeared than an attempt to choose a different posture within it.

notes.title: The sound of a parting warning
notes.body: 出门在外 means being away from home, where familiar protection and rules no longer apply. 要多加小心 has the sound of advice offered before somebody leaves. The next warning is about listening rather than physical danger, so the main hazard of the outside world becomes other people’s words.

notes.title: Speech loses its speaker
notes.body: People disappear into tongues and saliva. The sentence makes gossip physically excessive before it names any particular accusation: there are simply too many mouths producing too much material. It also makes the following wish for one’s “own voice” concrete. A voice carries a person; these disembodied tongues mostly produce spray.

notes.title: Travel without losing your voice
notes.body: The advice permits movement: go out, see the world, enjoy its scenery. Its condition is to keep your own voice. This is not a demand for isolation or purity. It allows curiosity while resisting the pressure to become another version of the surrounding chatter, a distinction that gives the track’s title its tension.

notes.title: A shared lack of innocence
notes.body: 干净 moves easily from physical cleanliness to an unblemished moral record. “Everyone is the same” first sounds conciliatory, then becomes an accusation that nobody is innocent. The shift checks the speaker’s earlier authority too: a song warning about other people’s speech includes itself in the compromised crowd.

notes.title: Quiet becomes a classroom
notes.body: 乖乖 is the affectionate but controlling language of telling children to behave. The orderly row prepares the later classroom question, bringing school discipline into a song about speech. What begins as the sensible wish for less gossip now risks becoming a demand that everyone be quiet and obedient.

notes.title: An intentionally crude idiom
notes.body: 脱裤子放屁 is a deliberately ridiculous image of doing an unnecessary extra step. It often works as the first half of a saying whose answer is simply 多此一举, needless effort. Here the missing explanation is supplied by the comic picture itself. After several measured lines of advice, that bodily vulgarity punctures the speaker’s almost elder-like tone.

phrase.en: drop your pants just to fart

notes.title: A toxic atmosphere, literally smoke and miasma
notes.body: 乌烟瘴气 combines dark smoke with foul, unhealthy air, and describes a disordered or morally unpleasant atmosphere. The translation gives the social effect; the Chinese still pictures something one has to breathe. It also lets the crude fart joke contaminate the whole surrounding space.

notes.title: The secret is who will say it
notes.body: A secret everyone knows is not hidden information; it is information governed by an agreement not to say it aloud. The next lines wait for someone else to raise the question in class. That turns the classroom into a small social system where knowledge can be common while the risk of speaking is left to another person.

notes.title: Two images of the almost impossible
notes.body: 铁树开花 is an idiom for something exceptionally rare; the “iron tree” names a cycad rather than a tree made of metal. The next example, the sun rising in the west, shifts from extreme rarity to the reversal of ordinary nature. Pairing them turns hopeful waiting into a joke about how impossible the desired change feels.

sources.label: Taiwan Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency: cycads

phrase.en: an iron tree coming into bloom

notes.title: An impossible case study

phrase.en: the sun rising in the west

notes.body: The expression is used for a reversal so surprising it would overturn the normal order of things. 案例, “case” or “example,” gives this impossible event a dry, almost report-like label. After wishing for a miracle, the voice briefly sounds as though it could enter one in a file and wait for precedent.

tracks.intro: Advice about finding your own voice curdles into gossip, compulsory quiet and shared secrets. The final miracles would require the ordinary world to reverse itself.

notes.title: The wolf inside the insult
notes.body: 白眼狼 names someone who repays kindness with ingratitude or betrayal. The wolf is not merely dangerous; its offense is relational, because care has already been given. Pairing that insult with “can’t be trusted” for much of the opening makes the verdict arrive before the story. The later disclosure of his whereabouts supplies the breach behind that relentless judgment.

notes.title: An unusual expansion of an idiom
notes.body: 柴米油盐 names the basic household staples—firewood, rice, oil and salt. The line folds that phrase into 油盐不进, refusing all persuasion, literally letting neither oil nor salt in. The expanded version makes the other person resistant to the whole material language of ordinary life: nothing practical, familiar or necessary seems able to get through.

notes.title: The wrong people knew where he was
notes.body: 小伙伴 is a friendly, slightly childlike term for companions. Setting it beside “gave away my whereabouts” makes the intimacy accusatory. These were people close enough to know where he was, which is precisely why their betrayal mattered. The cute name survives after trust is gone, making it more bitter than a straightforward enemy label.

notes.title: A life treated as a debt
notes.body: 索 is to demand or exact something; 命 is life. The verb makes vengeance sound like collection, linking the threat to the monetary and personal accounting of “Debt.” Yet within a few lines the speaker says he need not act at all. The verse moves between personally enforcing the balance and imagining that a larger order will settle it.

notes.title: Sincerity is imagined as opening the body
notes.body: 掏心 is literally taking out the heart, but figuratively opening oneself with complete sincerity. The warning follows a threat to claim lives and is followed by the claim that nobody can be trusted. That placement makes emotional openness feel like bodily exposure.

notes.title: The other side of claiming a life

phrase.en: Love your life and treasure it

notes.body: 爱 and 惜 are close but not identical: loving life and taking care not to lose it. Between revenge threats and proverbial advice, the phrase briefly sounds like guidance for staying alive. The repeated 命 links self-preservation to the enemy’s life demanded earlier, making survival and menace parts of the same vocabulary.

notes.title: A motivational proverb inside a revenge song

phrase.en: Failure is the mother of success

notes.body: This is a version of the familiar maxim 失败是成功之母: failure can lead to success. In its surroundings, however, the lesson learned is distrust, and the next proverb promises that bad people will be punished by other bad people. A consoling saying is recruited into a sequence about surviving betrayal.

notes.title: A proverb about who checks whom
notes.body: 恶人自有恶人磨 promises that one bad person will eventually meet another capable of tormenting them. The repetition of 恶人 leaves justice morally impure: the punisher need not be good. The following appeal to heaven offers a second version of the same relief, allowing the speaker to imagine a reckoning without doing the work himself.

phrase.en: An evil person has another evil person to grind them down

notes.title: Real estate for the dead

phrase.en: New apartments in the underworld are on sale

notes.body: 新楼盘开售 is the language of a new property development opening for sale. 地府 relocates that sales pitch to the realm of the dead. Instead of merely wishing an enemy dead, the line treats their afterlife accommodation as a product ready to move.

notes.title: Cash intended for the afterlife
notes.body: 纸钱 here is ritual paper money burned for spirits or the dead, rather than ordinary banknotes. It follows the underworld property sale and precedes the borrowed lighter and fire. Knowing that use ties the apparently separate images of purchasing, death, paper, and burning together.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 紙錢

notes.title: An ordinary request with the wrong purpose
notes.body: This begins as a tiny ordinary request. The next line anticipates the ordinary explanation—smoking—only to replace it with arson. Coming straight after ritual paper money, the lighter is the hinge between a recognizable act of burning offerings and a wildly enlarged fire. Its mundane scale makes the jump more absurd.

notes.title: Anger takes a whole year
notes.body: The fire is assigned the length of an entire year. Instead of a momentary flare of anger, it becomes something that persists across seasons, answered soon afterward by “so many years” of still not understanding people. The extravagant duration gives distrust its own weather: this is anger imagined as a condition one lives through.

notes.title: Even revenge gets old
notes.body: 新鲜 can mean fresh, novel or surprising. The profane rhetorical remark sounds unimpressed, undercutting the spectacular revenge scene it has just produced. Before the cube arrives, the verse briefly treats the cycle of betrayal and threatened punishment as something tiresomely familiar, even when its imagery is fantastically excessive.

notes.title: People and a cube share “sides”
notes.body: 面 is a side or surface and also an aspect of a person. The final 魔方, Rubik’s cube, turns the familiar idea of a many-sided person into a manipulable puzzle. Years of acquaintance have not solved it. The cube also limits any single view: seeing one face clearly does not tell you what is happening on the others.

tracks.intro: A loop of distrust opens into underworld property sales and a borrowed lighter. The final cube makes the problem visual: a person has more faces than you can see at once.

notes.title: Resignation inside the easy life

phrase.en: get by one day at a time

notes.body: 得过且过 means muddling through as long as one can, without ambitious plans or a strong sense of purpose. It often carries criticism of that attitude. “One day at a time” sounds gentler in English; the Chinese leaves more room for both deliberate ease and resignation.

notes.title: Ease as something earned
notes.body: 潇洒 suggests an unencumbered, stylish ease; 自如 adds being able to act naturally and comfortably. The following insistence that this road was walked by the speaker himself makes the ease an achievement. The song can sound resigned in 得过且过 and proud here without changing its practical aim: retaining control of the scale of one’s life.

notes.title: Visitors do not own the road
notes.body: 过客 is a traveler passing through a place, extended to someone who occupies only a temporary part of a life. The word redraws the relationship: critics who speak as though they own a stake in the speaker are only visitors. It also makes the earlier “road” image social, with people encountered along it but no obligation to keep traveling together.

notes.title: Company counted in bowls and chopsticks
notes.body: 碗筷 pairs bowl and chopsticks into a household place setting. Refusing extra company becomes a rule about the table: there is no equipment for an additional guest. The preceding “she” makes the space feel occupied rather than empty. The scene’s comfort depends on keeping an intimate household small, not on proving that the speaker needs absolutely nobody.

notes.title: Being remembered is not always comforting
notes.body: 惦记 can mean keeping someone fondly in mind, worrying about them, or having one’s eye on something one wants. The surrounding refusal of extra company makes the attention unwelcome. English “thinking of me” preserves the openness of the word without deciding whether these people miss him or want something from him.

notes.title: The first half of a Buddhist saying
notes.body: The familiar saying continues with becoming a Buddha on the spot: even someone who has done wrong can turn toward good. The lyric stops after laying down the knife, then moves to being at ease and sleeping peacefully. A moral turning point becomes the threshold to an ordinary, restful life.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 放下屠刀，立地成佛

notes.title: A duck in the title, a fish in the lyric
notes.body: 如鱼得水 means finding the environment or companion in which one can flourish: the fish finally has its water. The official English title substitutes a duck, an idiomatic choice in English, while the lyric preserves the fish. Here the ideal environment turns out to be a life without interference, with enough security to fall asleep easily.

sources.label: Ministry of Education idiom dictionary: 如魚得水

notes.title: The body measures success
notes.body: The reward is unusually modest: no anxiety and the ability to sleep. Across the mixtape, sleeplessness, bodily tension and overthinking repeatedly interrupt boasts. This line supplies their quiet opposite. Being at home in one’s life is tested by what the body can do when nobody is watching, rather than by what an audience applauds.

notes.title: A repetition worth keeping
notes.body: 又 makes recurrence explicit: another year, then another day. Paired with the same sleeping position, time becomes stable repetition instead of progress up a ladder. The intimacy with the pillow gives that repetition warmth. What might look monotonous from outside is presented as a routine safe enough to keep returning to.

notes.title: An intimate idiom applied to a pillow
notes.body: 如胶似漆 compares intimacy to glue and lacquer sticking together; it usually describes people inseparably close. Giving that relationship to a pillow makes the bed a comic partner. After rejecting extra companions and praising ease, the verse finds an attachment that asks for no explanation, no performance and no extra place at the table.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 如膠似漆

tracks.intro: Independence is measured in spare bowls, a closed front door and easy sleep. Grand sayings find their ideal environment in a very ordinary bed.

notes.title: Who controls the movement
notes.body: 步步 doubles “step” so that each movement adds pressure. Its clipped four-character shape faces the bodily loss of control in the next line. Repeating this pair makes intimidation mechanical: one person controls the pace, the other cannot control even their own body. The later demand to kneel completes that unequal choreography.

notes.title: Fear arrives before the laugh
notes.body: 还没…呢 emphasizes that an expected action has not even happened yet. The opponent is already crying before the speaker begins to laugh, so the taunt presents fear as premature and excessive. It is a small contest over timing: the threatening figure claims not only greater strength, but the power to decide when the scene has truly started.

notes.title: A threat denies its own effect
notes.body: This psychiatric term is deployed as a taunt immediately after threats and fear. The speaker first creates pressure, then frames the other person’s alarm as something wrong with them. That reversal is the line’s cruelty. It belongs to the voice’s manipulation of the scene, rather than functioning as a diagnosis of anybody in it.

notes.title: A feature priced in bitcoin
notes.body: A guest verse becomes a unit of cryptocurrency: one feat, one bitcoin. The English music-industry abbreviation drops straight into the Chinese sentence, treating the international feature economy as ordinary vocabulary. The deliberately enormous-sounding price establishes distance from the person asking. A few lines later, “I still don’t have much money” punctures the fantasy of effortless wealth.

notes.title: Making the rival smaller
notes.body: 弟 already places someone below an older brother; 娃 adds the diminutive sense of a child. The regionally flavored address makes the feature-price boast sound like an older figure brushing off an inexperienced youngster. The insult is about rank as much as money: the other person is too small to negotiate on equal terms.

notes.title: No role left for you
notes.body: 没有戏 literally says there is no play or performance; colloquially it means something has no prospect of working out. Here it dismisses the other person’s chances immediately after pricing a feature. It need not mean that a literal stage role has been refused.

notes.title: A specific name behind “caveman”
notes.body: 山顶洞人 is the Chinese name for the prehistoric humans associated with the Upper Cave at Zhoukoudian, near Beijing. In this taunt, that recognizable name is compressed into “caveman,” then coupled with ritual dancing. The historical term supplies the image; the verse is not describing an archaeological practice.

sources.label: Chinese Academy of Sciences: Zhoukoudian Upper Cave research

notes.title: 套路 means a routine—and a ploy
notes.body: 套路 can mean an organized set of moves and, colloquially, a predictable maneuver or manipulative ploy. After the wriggling, silk-spitting spectacle fails to affect him, the speaker asks for simpler 套路. The word makes the display sound rehearsed rather than powerful.

notes.title: A limit inside the excess
notes.body: 底线 is a lowest boundary or basic limit. Placed after extravagant threats and the admission of not having much cash, it separates performative excess from the speaker’s claim to personal standards. The nearby 套路, tricks or maneuvers, are what he sees through; the 底线 is what he says he will keep.

notes.title: A sudden turn to the dinner table
notes.body: 三鲜 means “three delicacies.” 地三鲜 is the familiar combination of eggplant, potato, and green pepper; 素三鲜 means a vegetarian trio, with the exact ingredients left unspecified here. After intimidation and the bitcoin feature price, the choice is suddenly an ordinary meal, followed by turning the serving tray and letting others eat first.

sources.label: CCTV 天天饮食: 地三鲜 ingredients and preparation

notes.title: The god observes table manners

phrase.en: Go ahead and dig in first

notes.body: Chinese table conversation can refer to beginning a meal as “moving the chopsticks.” After commanding somebody to kneel, the same voice now yields the first move to others at a shared table. The rotating serving tray, indecision over vegetables and small courtesy abruptly bring the self-styled god down to an ordinary communal meal.

notes.title: A familiar song phrase enters the chant

phrase.en: The light of the righteous path

notes.body: 正道的光 is recognizable from Huang Bo’s song 正义之道, documented in CCTV’s performance archive. Here its vocabulary of righteousness joins the black-and-white taiji image and the repeated “Lord Kai.” A phrase associated with moral uplift becomes part of an exaggerated personal coronation after the verse’s intimidation, bodily comedy and ordinary meal.

sources.label: CCTV: Huang Bo performs 正义之道

notes.title: The black-and-white diagram
notes.body: 太极 is not limited to the martial art called tai chi in English. The explicit black and white also evoke the taiji diagram, a circle of interlocking yin and yang halves. That gives the line a compact visual emblem rather than necessarily describing someone doing exercises.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 太極圖

notes.title: Kai becomes a title
notes.body: 凯 is the Kai in Zhang Zhengkai, Jackzebra’s name; 神 turns it into a godlike title. In colloquial praise, 神 also marks someone as a master or impossibly good performer. Repeating 凯神 after the “righteous path” and black-and-white taiji imagery stages a compact self-coronation, made more comic by how recently the voice was occupied with ordering vegetables.

sources.label: Apple Music: 青楼 songwriting credits

tracks.intro: Intimidation swerves into a restaurant order, ritual spectacle and a chant of self-coronation. The voice keeps choosing when to menace, shrug and let others eat first.

notes.title: Money as an exit
notes.body: 就 makes the sequence immediate: once the money is in hand, leave. The hook never stays to enjoy what has been acquired. Repetition makes cash feel less like a destination than permission to escape, a pattern sharpened by the later account of having to fight for a living.

notes.title: Trading up, with weapons as the image
notes.body: 鸟枪换炮 swaps a modest hunting gun for a cannon, an idiom for a dramatic improvement in means or circumstances. The scale of that upgrade contrasts with the later need to scrape together a meal. In between, the “secret” cannot be shared: the song puts the visible result of advancement next to the hidden means of obtaining it.

phrase.en: trading a musket for a cannon

notes.title: An identity worn by a car
notes.body: 套 here concerns using another vehicle’s registration identity, hence the translation’s “cloned” plates. Naming Hong Kong and Macau makes the image geographically specific; the vehicle wears credentials that do not straightforwardly belong to it. Coming after the secret of upgrading, that borrowed exterior prepares the later attack on an ugly 嘴脸, the face someone puts on.

sources.label: Shandong court: explanation of 套牌 in a plate-sharing case

notes.title: The same two characters, reversed
notes.body: 错过, cuòguò, is a missed opportunity; 过错, guòcuò, is a mistake or wrongdoing. Swapping the same two syllables turns the question from what one failed to get into what one did wrong. Set beside “good” and “evil,” the little reversal makes morality and opportunity sound disturbingly close: the words change place as easily as the excuses do.

notes.title: Owning both sides of the argument
notes.original: 好话赖话都被你说完了

phrase.zh: 好话赖话都被你说完了
phrase.en: You've said every nice thing and every nasty thing

notes.body: 好话 and 赖话 place favorable and unfavorable speech in the same person’s mouth. 说完了 suggests they have used up both sides, leaving no position they have not already occupied. The accusation is not simply dishonesty; it is opportunistic flexibility, immediately reduced to the need to secure a bite to eat.

notes.title: A meal stands for a livelihood
notes.body: 讨口饭 or 讨口饭吃 can mean scraping out a living. The small mouthful makes basic subsistence the scale of the effort. Beside the insistence on getting money and running, it keeps the cash imagery tied to survival as well as ambition.

notes.title: Who gets to frame the struggle

phrase.en: what it looks like to fight to survive

notes.body: 拼命 means exerting oneself desperately, with 命, life, embedded in the effort to live. That effort becomes an image captured by somebody else. The line introduces an asymmetry between doing the exhausting work and possessing a picture of it, preparing the later sales patter to sound like someone marketing another person’s struggle.

notes.title: A weather forecast for a face
notes.body: 局部多云 is “partly cloudy,” the phrasing of a weather report. Applying it to 脸色, facial appearance or expression, turns a bad mood into a forecast.

notes.title: Exhaustion before judgment

phrase.en: Of course you get lazy when you're too exhausted

notes.body: 自然 makes the connection sound self-evident: too much exhaustion produces inactivity. The sentence reverses the usual moral accusation that laziness explains a person’s difficulties. Here depletion comes first. Its ordinary, almost practical tone interrupts the more theatrical boasts and gives the song’s bad mood a bodily cause.

notes.title: The sound of a clearance sale
notes.body: 全场清仓 and 大甩卖 are the language of a shop clearing stock: everything must go. Later, 走过路过不要错过 calls out to passersby. Placing those public sales calls amid private exhaustion makes suffering sound as though it has been put on display. The speaker keeps getting money and running, while the lyric keeps breaking into sales patter.

notes.title: The bait meets somebody who will not bite
notes.body: 老奸巨猾 describes someone deeply practiced in deceit or cunning. There is no fox in the Chinese; English supplies its own familiar animal for that character. With a loach held at the mouth in the previous line, 不会咬 works both as refusing food and refusing to be lured in.

notes.title: The body stores what cannot be said

phrase.en: Pain with no outlet turns into fat

notes.body: 苦 is hardship, suffering, and bitterness; 脂肪 gives it a bodily storage place. The image makes blocked expression accumulate as matter. It belongs with the cloudy face and flashing body in the surrounding verse: what cannot be released in words returns as a surface or signal that others can see.

notes.title: A body told to stop and go
notes.body: The body becomes a traffic signal while it is barely managing to stay upright. Red and green offer incompatible instructions—stop and go—so the image fits a person required to continue while showing signs of strain. The next hawker call urges people not to miss the spectacle, making private warning signs into public attraction.

notes.title: A hard mouth and an uneasy heart
notes.body: 嘴硬 is refusing to concede or continuing to talk tough despite contrary evidence. The next line’s 心虚 is inward unease, guilt, or lack of confidence. Together they split the person into a defiant mouth and an insecure interior; the praise of how “cool” and “beautiful” this looks carries a mocking edge.

notes.title: Grey is also something that covers you
notes.body: 灰 means grey as a color, but also dust or ash as matter. 一身灰 coats the whole body with it. The title therefore becomes something lived on the skin, after cloudy expressions and flashing red-green signals have made emotion visible. It also answers the earlier neat questions about good and evil with a body that is anything but cleanly divided.

tracks.intro: Money, moral judgment and street-market patter collide. Exhaustion becomes weather on a face, a warning light in a body and finally a coating of grey dust.

notes.title: Reading the heat on a face
notes.body: The song opens with bodily discomfort before offering social advice. Later it tells the listener not to cry when the heat makes them sweat, blurring two kinds of moisture on a face. That small confusion prepares a track where expressions are unreliable and it is difficult to tell what people genuinely feel.

notes.title: A warning makes its own defense

phrase.en: If you hear it and don't remember

notes.body: 听 and 记 distinguish receiving words from retaining them. The advice demands both, then insults the listener who fails. This is guidance with pressure built into it: experience is transmitted as a warning, and any later suffering can be blamed on the person who did not remember the rules.

notes.title: Art is answered with a lack of skill
notes.body: 艺术, yìshù, ends with the same shù that closes 不学无术, bùxué-wúshù: having neither learning nor skill. The reply seizes the last sound of “art” and returns it as an accusation of incompetence. English carries the contempt but loses this quick verbal catch, where the lofty claim supplies the material for its own dismissal.

notes.title: Clarity becomes a costume
notes.body: 清白 means innocent or untainted, literally clear and white. It follows 清醒, being clearheaded, and precedes the accusation of pretending to be innocent. The shared 清, qīng, sound briefly builds an image of clarity before the next lines expose it as an act. The sequence lets pristine language do the work of camouflage.

notes.title: Indistinguishable faces become matching tiles
notes.body: 连连看 is a tile-matching game: identify repeated pictures and pair them away. It arrives immediately after “they all look the same,” making the surrounding people seem as interchangeable as game pieces. The narrator’s small private pastime becomes a way to judge a scene full of supposedly distinctive personalities.

sources.label: Developer description: 連連看 on Google Play

notes.title: Inspecting the scene as merchandise
notes.body: The phrase sounds like the heading of a sober report. Surrounded by judgments of faces, manners and rotten hearts, it turns watching a social scene into inspecting merchandise. The later gold-and-rotten-stuffing proverb returns to exactly that problem: what the polished exterior advertises versus what the thing contains.

notes.title: The body beneath the respectable face

phrase.en: Organs with nowhere to run wild

notes.body: 撒野 is behaving wildly or acting out without restraint. Giving that impulse to organs strips away the people’s respectable faces and leaves frustrated bodily drives. The line follows malice stored up for half a lifetime, so the behavior appears as pressure seeking an outlet rather than as an impressive form of freedom.

notes.title: Why keep “jianghu” in English?
notes.body: 江湖, jiānghú, literally means rivers and lakes, but also names the wider social world a person has to navigate. It carries the sense of informal rules, experience and entanglement captured in the saying about not being free to act as one pleases within it. Here that world becomes a poison: belonging has entered people’s bodies and altered them.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 江湖

notes.title: A fragment left unresolved
notes.body: 水帘洞, Water Curtain Cave, is the hidden home reached through a waterfall in the first chapter of Journey to the West. Entering it establishes the stone monkey’s authority among the other monkeys. The name brings that childhood-familiar fantastic space into a verse of smoke and half-sleep; it offers a refuge-like image just after the claim that the social world has poisoned people.

sources.label: Journey to the West, chapter 1 (Shidetang edition)

notes.title: Change without improvement
notes.body: This familiar announcement often promises modernization or progress. The next two lines make its conclusion simply that things are worse. The deadpan turn refuses to let novelty count as improvement, just as the song refuses to let a polished look count as inner worth. The speaker’s test is what the change does to people.

notes.title: A polished exterior and rotten stuffing
notes.body: This phrase comes from Liu Ji’s parable of an orange seller: beautiful fruit contains pulp as dry as worn cotton wadding, and the seller compares it to impressive-looking officials who fail the people. Its everyday meaning is an attractive exterior hiding poor substance. Here it caps a catalog of innocent faces and respectable appearances, giving the judgment a long satirical ancestry.

sources.label: Ministry of Education idiom dictionary: 金玉其外，敗絮其中

phrase.en: Gold and jade outside, rotten stuffing within

notes.title: An exasperated form of address
notes.body: 小祖宗, “little ancestor,” addresses someone with a mixture of fondness, deference and exasperation, as if the troublesome younger person must be served like an honored elder. After dismissing an entire crowd as ruined, the speaker suddenly sounds worried about a particular person. The maze and the failed rescue that follow make the affection hurt rather than simply soften the insult.

notes.title: The social world has no clear exit
notes.body: Unlike an open road, a maze offers movement without a clear way out. One careless entrance traps the person; seeing their stumbling from outside does not give the narrator a route to rescue them. This is the song’s most sympathetic image of jianghu: a social world can ruin someone without that person fully understanding its layout.

notes.title: Wanting to help is not being able to

phrase.en: there's nothing I can do to help

notes.body: The segmentation is 可 / 爱莫能助: “but / willing to help yet unable to.” 可爱 is not “cute” here. The idiom preserves the speaker’s concern even as it admits powerlessness, which makes the following physical and emotional withdrawal more conflicted than a simple refusal to care.

notes.title: Three kinds of distance
notes.body: 隔离 repeats after three modifiers: physical, biological, emotional. The technical-sounding sequence makes withdrawal resemble a procedure carried out in stages. Yet it follows “I see all of your pain” and “I cannot help,” so the final emotional separation is the hardest step. Distance is being constructed because care alone has not made rescue possible.

notes.title: 骚 is wider than its literal sexual sense
notes.body: 骚, sāo, can describe sexual boldness, but colloquial praise also uses it for conspicuous flair or an outrageous move. “Flashy” captures that showy excess. After the long withdrawal into emotional isolation, the short exclamations suddenly sound like a spectator reacting to somebody’s display, with admiration and mockery still entangled.

tracks.intro: A warning about the social world becomes a consumer report on its damaged people. The speaker moves between contempt, worried affection and the decision to withdraw.

notes.title: A prediction presented as fact
