notes.body: Calling the opening a “fact” asserts authority before presenting any evidence. The following future-tense pursuit cannot yet be observed, but the phrase asks us to receive it as settled. That certainty shapes the entire chant: escape, luck and disbelief are all ruled out by a voice speaking as if the outcome has already happened.

notes.title: Vanity becomes the target
notes.body: 狙击 means a targeted or sniper-like strike; its target here is explicitly vanity. The threatened strike targets the wish to be admired rather than the body. The following promise to keep someone in a dream turns that weakness into a means of capture: flattery can immobilize as effectively as a threat.

notes.title: Luck and effort are set against each other
notes.body: 侥幸 especially suggests obtaining a good outcome or escaping trouble by chance. The following “no escape” makes that shade stronger than generic good fortune. Later, the speaker says he has kept working and fighting; the song grants others no lucky exit while claiming his own position through effort.

notes.title: A cheerful confectionery name over a threat
notes.body: HARIBO’s name brings the world of gummy sweets and colorful packaging into the title. The verse then names cotton candy and bubble gum before dismantling the sweetness into flavoring and color. The point is less a particular product than the distance between an inviting surface and what has been manufactured to produce it.

notes.title: Sweetness listed as ingredients
notes.body: 香精 and 色素 are flavoring and coloring, the technical ingredients behind an appealing taste and appearance. 堆在一起, simply piled together, drains that appeal of craft or mystery. After vanity and the dream, the sweets offer a concrete model for a seductive illusion: the attractive whole is made from effects designed to be consumed.

notes.title: 命 as fate
notes.body: 命, mìng, can mean life or fate. 这就是 makes the verdict categorical: this is what has been assigned to you. The next “believe it or not” denies the listener a meaningful role in deciding it. The song’s speaker then claims his own position through effort, producing a sharp asymmetry between another person’s fixed fate and his own active struggle.

notes.title: A choice that changes nothing
notes.body: The formula literally leaves belief up to you, but gives no choice over the outcome itself. Its apparent freedom is narrow: the listener can disagree internally while the predicted fate proceeds. That makes it a fitting answer to the title’s inviting candy image—acceptance can be offered without changing the trap.

notes.title: Effort keeps moving
notes.body: 拼 is striving with everything one has, sometimes with the sense of putting oneself at risk. 一直在 keeps that effort in progress. After a verse that immobilizes somebody else in a dream, the speaker identifies himself through ongoing work; “number one” is presented as the outcome of motion, not simply an attractive image.

tracks.intro: Vanity gets a candy coating, then hardens into fate. A compact chant pits manufactured sweetness against the speaker’s repeated claim to work and effort.

notes.title: An ordinary start leaves room for care
notes.body: The opening uses a few unadorned pieces of routine: afternoon, waking up, a call, a message. The confidence that every problem can be settled is built on those small actions. That ordinary scale makes the later direct plea to survive more intimate; the song begins close enough to daily life for care to arrive without a grand introduction.

notes.title: Invulnerability in four characters
notes.body: 百毒不侵 literally declares that a hundred poisons cannot get in; 百 means all kinds rather than a counted list. It gives emotional resilience the form of bodily immunity. The preceding phone call and message make that enormous claim funny: everyday problem-solving is narrated with the invulnerability of a mythic body.

notes.title: Calm as a surface of water
notes.body: 波澜 are waves or ripples, here transferred to the inner life. The speaker describes stillness immediately after firm will and immunity to poison, creating a picture of total composure. Later boredom becomes stifling and other people cannot stop. The image of calm is something the song has to preserve against a much noisier social environment.

notes.title: Not knowing the world can preserve something
notes.body: 见世面 means acquiring social experience and seeing how the wider world works. The next line gives the resulting naivety the unexpectedly approving description “pure.” Later, the speaker sees the social scene clearly enough to want to become invisible, complicating the idea that more exposure is always better.

notes.title: A blessing measured by appetite
notes.body: 福气 is the good fortune of a life going well. Its measure here is simply being able to eat and drink. That bodily minimum sits far below the money, fashion and rank flaunted elsewhere on the mixtape. The instruction to keep living grows out of this modest definition of a good life, rather than out of a demand to achieve more.

notes.title: What the request actually asks
notes.body: 活下去 means continuing to live; 好好的 adds care, safety and doing it well. The repeated 好 and the polite 请 give the command tenderness. It is not just endurance at any cost. Addressed to 老兄弟, an old friend, the line asks for the person’s continued presence before asking anything about success, usefulness or public recognition.

notes.title: An address to a longstanding companion
notes.body: 老 can mark familiarity or longstanding closeness rather than advanced age; 兄弟 often addresses a male friend or companion. The repeated address makes the plea to keep living feel personally directed. It need not identify a biological sibling.

notes.title: The substance is not named
notes.body: 吸, xī, means to inhale or suck; in this social scene it insinuates drug use without naming a substance. Crucially, 我猜 means “I guess.” The line stages the speaker making a judgment from appearances—ear studs and gold teeth—then refusing further details. Keeping that distance matters more than filling the omission with a specific drug.

notes.title: Caught between laughing and crying
notes.body: 哭笑不得 describes a situation too absurd or uncomfortable for either laughter or tears to feel adequate. Both responses are named and both withheld. Between stifling boredom and being speechless, the phrase makes reaction itself difficult: the speaker can observe the scene but cannot find a comfortable way to participate in it.

phrase.en: Don't know whether to laugh or cry

notes.title: A spectator who wants a screen
notes.body: The scene feels so strange that watching acquaintances becomes like watching another genre of reality. This is not the director’s control claimed in “Poker Face”: the speaker sits beside the action and wants nobody to address him. The film comparison places a screen between observer and participants, preparing the wish to become transparent.

notes.title: Transparency as an escape from contact
notes.body: 透明 means transparent, and the following wish explains its social purpose: nobody would stop him to talk or ask irrelevant questions. The fantasy is the reverse of demanding attention. After instructing a friend to value their existence, the speaker imagines relief in making his own presence unavailable to the surrounding crowd.

notes.title: The relief of having no role
notes.body: 局 is a situation, arrangement or game; a 局外人 stands outside it. The next identities shrink further, from an unknown little person to an unnoticed passerby. That descending list makes anonymity desirable, a way to escape being enlisted in the romances, questions and habits of a scene that already feels exhausting.

notes.title: 小人 does not have to mean villain
notes.body: 小人 can condemn somebody as petty or dishonorable, as in “Debt.” Here it is surrounded by being unknown, outside the group, and unnoticed, so the size meaning—an insignificant little person—fits the self-description better. The same two characters can serve contempt or self-effacement depending on their neighbors.

notes.title: Reassurance alongside indifference
notes.body: 无所谓 can dismiss a question as unimportant or announce that one no longer cares about its answer. It follows a passage full of painful observation and an earlier plea to keep living. Repetition therefore sounds like an attempt to maintain a boundary, rather than proof of effortless indifference: the voice keeps saying “whatever” because the scene keeps demanding a response.

notes.title: Yang Kun’s “无所谓” is inside this refrain

phrase.en: Who falls in love with whom

notes.body: The sequence of indifference, falling in love and wearing someone down reworks the opening of Yang Kun’s “无所谓.” Here its familiar romantic resignation follows the desire to disappear from a social scene. Borrowing an already recognizable refrain supplies a ready-made way to say something the verse has struggled to express: other people’s entanglements do not have to become his own.

sources.label: JOOX: Yang Kun, 无所谓 (lyrics and credits)
CCTV: Yang Kun performs 无所谓

tracks.intro: A casual afternoon turns into a plea for an old friend to keep living. Withdrawal follows, but the borrowed “whatever” refrain never quite erases that care.

notes.title: Too late to get an early night
notes.original: 趁闹钟还没响的时候早点睡

phrase.zh: 趁闹钟还没响的时候早点睡
phrase.en: Get some sleep before the alarm goes off

notes.body: 早点睡 normally means going to bed early, sensible advice for a normal evening. “Before the alarm goes off” relocates it to the last scraps of a sleepless night. The everyday phrase becomes darkly comic because the opportunity to follow it has almost passed; the next insistence on continuous thinking explains why rest is so hard to reach.

notes.title: Lost inside camouflage
notes.body: 迷彩, mícǎi, is camouflage; 迷茫, mímáng, is feeling lost. Both begin with mí, the sound of confusion or being led astray. Writing the second across the first makes the outfit announce the feeling it might otherwise hide. The following “battle-worn without a battlefield” continues that split between a military exterior and a less visible source of distress.

notes.title: A soldier’s exterior without a battle
notes.body: 沧桑, cāngsāng, compresses an older image of seas becoming fields: a world changed beyond recognition. It describes a person worn by experience, not only by war. Translating it as “battle-worn” catches the neighboring camouflage and battlefield, but the lyric’s point is that the wear exists even without the recognized event that would explain it.

sources.label: Ministry of Education idiom dictionary: 滄海桑田

notes.title: A hard center inside fatigue
notes.body: The spine supplies a hard, upright center after exhaustion, camouflage and unseen enemies. An indestructible backbone is a bodily boast, but its placement also reads as the determination not to bend. The song moves from being worn out to imagining a part of the self that cannot be made weak, preparing the turn from inward fatigue to outward attack.

notes.title: One word moves from exhausted to destructive
notes.body: The opening’s 废 describes feeling useless or spent; 废了 here becomes something the speaker will do to other people’s mouths—ruin or disable them. The shared word converts a state of personal depletion into an outward threat, still directed at speech rather than an identified opponent.

notes.title: Huddling for warmth becomes a clique
notes.body: 抱团取暖 is huddling together for warmth, an image of survival through mutual support. Repeated 依旧, “still,” makes the little cliques seem entrenched rather than newly formed. The accusation is that the circle perpetuates itself. Beside the scams later in the song, solidarity sounds less like an open offer of help than a protection scheme for insiders.

notes.title: Drunk with disbelief
notes.body: 我也是醉了, literally “I’m drunk too,” became a conversational expression of exasperation or disbelief: the equivalent of “I can’t even.” It lets the speaker react to something absurd by describing his own helplessness. In a verse opened by fatigue, the stock joke briefly returns the aggressive voice to being overwhelmed.

notes.title: A rich person—or a game?
notes.body: 大富翁 is both a very wealthy person and the name of property-and-money games, including the Richman series. The next line brings in anti-addiction language, activating the game association. The title “Monoplay” fits that field of play without naming a particular game. Wealth and competitive absorption sit together, making accumulation look like a pastime someone cannot stop.

notes.title: The vocabulary of stopping a game
notes.body: 防沉迷, fáng chénmí, is familiar from systems intended to limit excessive online gaming, including official rules for minors. It is not a new legal idea waiting to be invented. Following 大富翁, the phrase gives the verse’s rich people or game players the vocabulary of a monitored habit, turning accumulation into something that might need an enforced stopping point.

sources.label: National Press and Publication Administration: anti-addiction gaming notice (2021)

notes.title: A regional word for chili
notes.body: 海椒, hǎijiāo, is a regional word for chili used in Sichuan and neighboring areas. “Chili” gets the ingredient across but loses the local voice. Placing it beside kangaroo meat makes a comic meeting of the distant and familiar: an unusual food is approached with the everyday seasoning vocabulary of home.

sources.label: Linguistic study: regional words for chili peppers

notes.title: A brand name that also sounds self-absorbed
notes.body: 自嗨锅 is the Zihaiguo self-heating meal brand. 自嗨, zìhāi, also means entertaining oneself or getting excited inside one’s own bubble. Calling the meal expired makes a shelf-life judgment double as a judgment on self-absorption. Coming after the little cliques, the convenience-food label becomes a compact joke about people impressed chiefly by themselves.

notes.title: Giving up respectability first
notes.body: 无赖 can describe a shameless rogue who refuses ordinary obligations or reasoning. After condemning cliques and deception, the speaker claims the disreputable label for himself. That removes one weapon from opponents: threatening his respectability has less force if he has already theatrically thrown it away. The laugh that follows enjoys that freedom.

notes.title: Outsourcing the reckoning

phrase.en: Heaven will collect you on its own

notes.body: 天, heaven, acts as the eventual enforcer; 收 makes the person sound ready to be taken away or collected. Repeating this after “I don’t even have to touch you” imagines revenge without direct effort. It reprises “Cube,” where the speaker also hands punishment upward, before returning here to meticulously personalized threats.

notes.title: Changing colors as self-defense
notes.body: 变色龙 is the chameleon, also a figure for somebody whose position changes opportunistically. The voice immediately turns that suspicious image into an advantage: switching colors prevents others from seeing through him. The creature that would usually expose somebody as unreliable becomes a way to resist being read or pinned down.

notes.title: A threat small enough for a bathroom
notes.body: 蛾蠓 names the tiny moth-like flies associated with damp drains. After the chameleon and a threat to blind the listener, this thoroughly unglamorous bathroom insect brings the menace close to everyday life. The image does not need a large predator: something small, intrusive and difficult to ignore can already make an ordinary room unpleasant.

notes.title: An insult claimed as an identity
notes.body: 奇葩 originally names an extraordinary flower, but conversationally it often describes a bizarre person or thing. “Freak” selects that latter force. The speaker embraces the label and places himself in another world, then immediately asks whether the listener is afraid to go home. His strangeness crosses from self-description into the listener’s most familiar space.

notes.title: The audience turns against the speaker
notes.body: A podium gives someone a height, an audience and a claim to authority. The threat is to expose that person in front of children until the audience laughs. It mirrors “Sunshine” by turning an instructional setting against its authoritative figure: the person who expects everyone to listen becomes the object everybody watches.

notes.title: The cover that hides disgrace
notes.body: 遮羞布 literally means a cloth covering shame, figuratively the respectable excuse or appearance hiding something disgraceful. English “fig leaf” replaces the material image with an equivalent idiom. Tearing it away on a podium turns exposure into a public event: the person’s authority collapses not through a counterargument, but through becoming laughable before the audience.

notes.title: The problem moves from sight to survival
notes.body: Muddy water makes seeing difficult, but the line answers with the ability to breathe. That shift changes the stakes from judging appearances to remaining alive within a hostile environment. The plural “we” briefly breaks the isolated self-mythology: the following lament for “my brothers” makes survival a shared condition, not only a personal boast.

notes.title: Avoiding work by being clever about it
notes.body: 偷奸耍滑 describes using sly tricks to avoid effort or responsibility. It is not the same as the outright fraud in the parallel line about scams. Keeping the two accusations distinct makes the repeated contempt target both active deception and opportunistic evasion.

notes.title: A familiar ritual road becomes a threat
notes.body: 上坟 means visiting a grave to pay respects, rather than simply being buried. The line bends that ordinary ritual journey into an ambush-like meeting place. After saying there is a long road ahead, the speaker supplies a destination that cancels the other person’s future; the wreath and payment details then turn the imagined aftermath into a carefully managed event.

notes.title: A triumphant phrase on the wrong road
notes.body: 高歌 and 猛进 recall the heroic idiom 高歌猛进, advancing vigorously while singing. In this funeral-bound sequence, the triumphant movement is grotesquely misplaced. A phrase suited to confidence and collective progress carries someone toward the grave scene instead, continuing the song’s habit of turning positive public language into a private taunt.

notes.title: The last detail is who paid
notes.body: The wreath supposedly arrives from the enemy’s beloved people, but the speaker interrupts himself to correct the account: he paid. Repeating that mundane detail steals control of the farewell from both mourners and dead person. After the grand threats, the final humiliation is administrative—he can claim the receipt for the tribute. It also recalls “Debt,” where relationships become entries in a ledger.

phrase.en: I'm the one who paid for it

tracks.intro: Fatigue puts on camouflage, then turns outward against cliques and scams. Games, convenience food and funeral logistics make the threats oddly familiar and domestic.

notes.title: “Your boy” is the speaker
notes.body: 哥, gē, is literally older brother, but as a self-reference it claims a relaxed seniority: “your boy,” with the implication that this speaker deserves recognition. It is different from the harsher 老子 later in the verse. The song can shift from teasing internet swagger to aggression simply by changing what the speaker calls himself.

notes.title: A swaggering line with an internet afterlife
notes.body: The longer slogan “don’t be obsessed with me; I’m only a legend” was already cataloged among 2009 internet catchphrases in a study hosted by East China Normal University. This line carries that recognizable boast, while the next asks to be treated as if the speaker never appeared. Legend and disappearance sit side by side.

sources.label: East China Normal University-hosted study, table of 2009 internet catchphrases

notes.title: A legend asks to disappear

phrase.en: Just act like I was never here

notes.body: The claim to legendary status is paired with a request for erasure. That combination lets the speaker enjoy recognition while refusing ordinary access to himself. Later, he explains why he cannot tell much of his story: others could use it. The hook’s disappearance is therefore more pointed than simple modesty after a boast.

notes.title: Hollow confidence versus a solid body
notes.body: 实 contrasts with the previous line’s 虚: solid or real versus hollow, shaky, or lacking confidence. The opposition works through both the body and credibility. A few lines later, having only half a yuan still does not prevent the speaker from carrying himself with style.

notes.title: Turning a proverb upside down
notes.original: 常走在河边脚都不湿的
notes.body: The familiar warning asks how anyone can keep walking by a river without getting their shoes wet: repeated exposure to trouble eventually catches up with you. This line grants the speaker exactly that impossible exemption. The boast is not that he avoids risky ground, but that the usual consequences fail to stick to him.

phrase.zh: 常走在河边脚都不湿的
phrase.en: I keep walking by the river and my feet never get wet

notes.title: Style without a budget
notes.body: 五毛 is fifty fen, half of one yuan: deliberately little pocket money. The next line insists that style survives that lack. Coming after claims to surpass everyone combined, this is an anti-flex inside the flex: the speaker makes charisma independent of expensive proof, just as “Poker Face” puts dignity before earnings.

notes.title: A regional question sharpens the challenge
notes.body: 咋个 is a colloquial, regionally marked way of asking “how.” 管 can mean manage, control, or interfere with someone. Here the whole question challenges the other people’s ability to police his behavior, rather than asking them for practical guidance.

notes.title: Fear of no longer counting
notes.body: 淘汰 is being eliminated, selected out or rendered obsolete. It makes the rivalry sound like a competitive process with losers who stop counting. The response is helpless anger at empty air, while the speaker watches from the side. His superiority is performed as freedom from the very contest that has made the others frantic.

notes.title: Watching drama as “eating melon”
notes.body: 吃瓜, chī guā, literally means eating melon; online it describes watching other people’s drama as a spectator. The preceding 看戏, watching a show, gives the same stance in an older image. Together they make detachment pleasurable: while the other person rages at thin air, the speaker settles in to enjoy the performance.

notes.title: Success makes a person usable
notes.body: 利用 means putting something to use and, with a person as object, taking advantage of them. The danger arrives at the point of greatest visibility, not at failure. That interrupts the earlier carefree cool: becoming more successful also makes one’s story useful material for others, giving the refusal to disclose it a protective purpose.

notes.title: A little person with a big pose
notes.body: 小卡拉米, xiǎo kǎlāmi, dismisses someone as an insignificant little character, roughly “small fry.” Its comic sound cuts the threatening social pose down to size before 社会, street toughness, inflates it again. Repeating the pairing lets the little nobody and the big pose keep colliding in the same breath.

notes.title: An intentionally elastic “society”
notes.body: 社会 ordinarily means society, but as a colloquial adjective it can praise or mock streetwise toughness. 社会很社会 uses the word in both positions, making the explanation deliberately circular: society is very “society.” Following the repeated dismissal of petty nobodies, the tautology mocks a scene whose claim to depth may consist mainly of its own tough label.

notes.title: The actual street beneath the swagger
notes.body: 坑坑洼洼 doubles pits and hollows into a bumpy four-syllable texture. After the repeated grand word “society,” the verse gives us a road that still cannot be repaired properly. The mundane failure punctures the surrounding performance of power: all that talk of being streetwise has not made the actual ground easier to travel.

notes.title: A witness who cannot be rushed
notes.body: Time is personified as the eventual witness. After restricting access to his story and asserting that he is real, the speaker postpones judgment to something less manipulable than the current crowd. The phrase promises vindication without supplying it now, before the hook returns to the paradox of becoming a legend and disappearing.

tracks.intro: Old internet swagger meets half a yuan, a potholed road and anxiety about being used. The voice claims to be a legend while asking to be left out of the record.

research.label: Education Ministry: prohibition on paid tutoring by serving schoolteachers (2015)
research.claims: The 2015 notice forbids schools and serving primary/secondary teachers from organizing or inducing pupils into paid supplementary classes; contextualizes the specific conflict in Sunshine, not an allegation about a real teacher.

research.label: Ministry of Education idiom dictionary: 金玉其外，敗絮其中
research.claims: Traces the saying to Liu Ji’s orange-seller parable, where handsome fruit with rotten interiors becomes criticism of officials with impressive standing and poor substance.

research.label: Ministry of Education idiom dictionary: 對牛彈琴
research.claims: Standard meaning addresses an uncomprehending audience; early story also concerns adapting one’s expression to an audience rather than only declaring that audience stupid.

research.label: National Press and Publication Administration: anti-addiction gaming notice (2021)
research.claims: 防沉迷 is an established policy/technical vocabulary concerning minors and online games; regulations existed before this song. The lyric’s question should not be presented as factual absence of law.

research.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 江湖
research.claims: Beyond rivers/lakes, 江湖 names the environment/social world one inhabits and occurs in the expression about being unable to act freely within it.

research.label: Tongling Daily: a primary school’s campaign against playground parodies (2007)
research.claims: School head describes children replacing the schoolbag in 上学歌 with an explosives bag and school-destruction lyrics; documents both oral circulation and adult objection. Does not establish an originator.

research.label: Nankai Youth League: jianbing rhyme (2017)
research.claims: Article uses the yo/check-it-out/jianbing-set rhyme, supporting recognition of the rewritten hawker chant in Coffin Baby.

research.label: Southern Weekly / Nanfang Plus: 嘻嘻不嘻嘻 (2024)
research.claims: Documents the paired meme expression as a switch from laughter to not laughing.

research.label: Ministry of Education idiom dictionary: 如魚得水
research.claims: The idiom includes finding a suitable environment or compatible person; its fish-water image is not the duck of the official English title.

research.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 如膠似漆
research.claims: Glue-and-lacquer image describes close, inseparable relationships; applying it to a pillow shifts that intimacy into a domestic object.

research.label: Apple Music: 青楼 songwriting credits
research.claims: Song credits identify jackzebra’s name as 张正凯; 凯 in 凯神 corresponds to Kai in his name, supporting the nickname explanation.

research.label: Taiwan Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency: cycads
research.claims: Identifies cycads as the plants commonly called 鐵樹; avoids treating the idiom as a tree literally made of iron.

research.label: Shandong court: explanation of 套牌 in a plate-sharing case
research.claims: Describes using another vehicle’s plate identity, supporting the language gloss in Grey; no legal advice or claims about an actual offense by the artist.

research.label: Linguistic study: regional words for chili peppers
research.claims: Research abstract locates 海椒 especially in Sichuan/Chongqing, supporting the regional language note; not evidence of travel or a specific meal.
